intro.title: Cybersecurity Basics
intro.subtitle: Simple habits that keep you and your organization safe
intro.say: Welcome to Cybersecurity Basics. Most attacks don't begin with brilliant hacking. They begin with a reused password, a rushed click, or a missed update. Over the next few minutes, we'll walk through thirteen areas, and the simple habits in each one that keep you, and your organization, safe.

sections.title: Passwords and Accounts
sections.say: Let's start with passwords and accounts. Your passwords are the keys to everything else.
items: Unique, long passphrase for every account
16+ characters
Use a unique, long passphrase for every account. Aim for sixteen characters or more.
Use a reputable password manager
No reusing, no sticky notes
Store your passwords in a reputable password manager, instead of reusing them or writing them down.
Turn on multi-factor authentication
Email, banking, and admin accounts first
Turn on multi-factor authentication, especially for email, banking, and admin accounts.
Prefer passkeys or hardware security keys
SMS codes can be intercepted
Where you can, choose passkeys or hardware security keys over text message codes, which can be intercepted.
Act on breach alerts
Change any password that appears in a leak
And watch for breach alerts. If a password shows up in a leak, change it right away.

sections.title: Phishing and Social Engineering
sections.say: Next, phishing and social engineering. Attackers know it's often easier to trick a person than to break a system.
items: Be suspicious of urgency
Money, credentials, or gift cards
Be suspicious of urgent requests for money, credentials, or gift cards. Pressure is the attacker's favorite tool.
Check the real sender and the real link
Hover before you click
Check the actual sender address, and hover over links before you click them.
Go to websites directly
Not through links in unexpected messages
Go to websites directly, rather than through links in unexpected emails or texts.
Verify unusual requests by calling back
Use a number you already know
Verify unusual requests by calling back on a number you already know, never one that's in the message.
Report suspicious messages
To IT or your email provider
And report suspicious messages to I.T., or to your email provider. Your report could protect everyone else.

sections.title: Devices and Software
items: Install security updates promptly
Browsers, operating systems, and VPNs
Install security updates promptly, especially for browsers, operating systems, and V P Ns.
Antivirus or EDR on every device
Endpoint detection and response
Run antivirus, or endpoint detection and response software, on every device.
Enable full-disk encryption
BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on Mac
Enable full disk encryption. That's Bit Locker on Windows, and File Vault on Mac.
Lock devices automatically
Require a PIN or biometric
Set devices to lock automatically, and require a pin or a biometric to get back in.
Remove software you no longer use
Every program adds attack surface
And remove software you no longer use. Every extra program is one more way in.

sections.title: Networks
items: Change default passwords
Routers and connected devices
Change the default passwords on your router, and on every connected device.
Use WPA3 or WPA2 on Wi-Fi
Keep guest networks separate
Use W P A three, or W P A two, on your Wi-Fi, and keep guest networks separate from business systems.
Use a firewall
Close the ports you don't need
Use a firewall, and close any ports you don't need.
Protect yourself on public Wi-Fi
VPN or zero-trust access
On public Wi-Fi, use a V P N, or a zero trust access tool in place of a traditional V P N.
Segment your network
One compromised device can't reach everything
And segment your network, so that one compromised device can't reach everything.

sections.title: Email Security
sections.say: Email security. Email is still the number one way attackers get in.
items: Set up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
Stops others from spoofing your domain
Set up S P F, dee kim, and dee mark for your domain. Together, they stop other people from spoofing your email address.
Filter spam and malware
Sandbox attachments where available
Enable spam and malware filtering, and sandboxing of attachments where it's available.
Check your forwarding rules
Attackers often add hidden ones
And disable any automatic forwarding rules you didn't create. Attackers often add them to quietly read your mail.

sections.title: Data Protection and Backups
sections.say: Data protection and backups. This is what saves you on your worst day.
items: Follow the 3-2-1 rule
3 copies · 2 media types · 1 off-site or offline
Follow the three, two, one rule. Three copies of your data, on two types of media, with one copy off site or offline.
Test your restores regularly
An untested backup is not a backup
Test your restores regularly. An untested backup is not a backup.
Keep one backup offline or immutable
Protection against ransomware
Keep at least one backup offline, or immutable, to protect against ransomware.
Encrypt sensitive data
At rest and in transit
Encrypt sensitive data, both at rest and in transit.
Limit access to sensitive data
Remove it when people leave
And limit who can access sensitive data. When people leave, remove their access.

sections.title: Access Control
items: Apply least privilege
Only the access the job requires
Apply least privilege. Give each person only the access their job requires.
Separate admin accounts
Never for daily email or browsing
Use separate admin accounts for administrative tasks, not for daily email and browsing.
Review access on a schedule
Including shared accounts
Review user access, and shared accounts, on a regular schedule.
Offboard the same day
Remove former employees' access immediately
And remove a former employee's access the same day they leave.

sections.title: Ransomware and Incident Response
sections.say: Ransomware and incident response. When something goes wrong, the first few minutes matter most.
items: Keep an incident response plan
Clear contacts and clear steps
Keep an incident response plan, with clear contacts, and clear steps.
Isolate infected machines right away
Disconnect from the network — don't power off
Isolate infected machines right away. Disconnect them from the network, but don't power them off. That preserves evidence.
Report the incident
IT provider, legal counsel, regulators if required
Report incidents to your I.T. provider, your legal counsel, and, where required, to regulators.
Keep logs for key systems
So you can investigate what happened
And keep logs for your key systems, so you can investigate what happened.

sections.title: Cloud and SaaS
sections.say: Cloud, and software as a service.
items: Enable MFA and audit logging
Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and others
Enable multi-factor authentication, and audit logging, on Microsoft three sixty five, Google Workspace, and your other cloud platforms.
Review sharing settings
No public links to sensitive files
Review your sharing settings, to prevent public links to sensitive files.
Monitor for unusual logins
New countries or impossible travel
Monitor for unusual log-ins, like a new country, or impossible travel between two places.
Check third-party apps
Anything with access to your email or files
And check the security settings of third party apps that have access to your email, or your files.

sections.title: Vendors and Supply Chain
sections.say: Vendors and the supply chain. Your security is only as strong as the companies you trust.
items: Vet vendors before sharing data
Ask about their security practices
Vet a vendor's security practices before you share data with them.
Limit and monitor third-party access
Only what they need
Limit third party access, and monitor it.
Watch trusted suppliers too
Compromised updates and unexpected changes
And watch for compromised software updates, and unexpected changes, even from suppliers you trust.

sections.title: Mobile Devices
items: Install apps only from official stores
And review app permissions
Install apps only from official stores, and review the permissions each app asks for.
Keep phones updated
Avoid jailbreaking or rooting
Keep your phone updated, and avoid jail breaking or rooting it.
Separate work and personal
Use profiles or containers where possible
And where possible, use separate work and personal profiles, or containers.

sections.title: Human Factors
sections.say: Human factors. Technology alone is never enough. People are the strongest defense.
items: Run regular awareness training
With simulated phishing tests
Run regular security awareness training, with simulated phishing tests.
Make reporting mistakes safe and easy
Fast reports beat hidden errors
Make reporting mistakes safe and easy, so people report quickly, instead of hiding errors.
Make verification normal
Even when the request comes from an executive
And create a culture where asking for verification is normal, even when the request comes from an executive.

sections.title: AI and Emerging Threats
sections.say: Finally, A.I. and emerging threats. Artificial intelligence is changing the game, for attackers and defenders alike.
items: AI-generated phishing
Good grammar is no longer a sign of safety
A.I. generated phishing. Attackers can now write convincing, error free messages at scale, so good grammar is no longer a reliable sign that a message is safe.
Deepfakes
Verify payment or account changes on a second channel
Deep fakes. Voices and video can be faked, so verify any payment or account change through a second, known channel.
Prompt injection
Limit what AI tools can do automatically
Prompt injection. Malicious instructions hidden in emails, web pages, or documents can manipulate the A.I. tools that read them. So limit what those tools are allowed to do automatically.
Data leakage to AI tools
No confidential data in unapproved AI services
Data leakage. Don't paste confidential client data, credentials, or proprietary code into public A.I. services, unless your organization has approved them.
Shadow AI
Set a clear policy and provide approved tools
Shadow A.I. Employees using unapproved A.I. apps can expose data. So set a clear A.I. use policy, and provide approved tools.
AI in defense
Supplements human review — doesn't replace it
A.I. in defense. It helps with threat detection, log analysis, and alert triage. But it should supplement human review, not replace it.
Verify AI output
It can be wrong, including insecure code
And verify A.I. output. It can make mistakes, or invent facts, including code with vulnerabilities. So review it before you rely on it.

outro.title: Security is a habit
outro.say: That's the basics. Remember, security isn't something you buy once. It's a set of small habits. Use strong, unique passwords with multi-factor authentication. Pause, and verify, before you click or pay. Keep your systems updated and backed up. And if something looks wrong, report it right away. Thanks for watching, and stay safe.
items: Strong, unique passwords + MFA
Pause and verify before you click or pay
Keep systems updated and backed up
See something wrong? Report it right away
